stories.headline: COP31 final day: nations split over fossil fuel cuts, finance and 35x35 goal
stories.summary: COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, entered its final day with negotiators still divided over the pace of fossil fuel cuts, the scale and delivery of climate finance, and a proposed 35x35 goal to raise electricity's share of total final energy use to 35% by 2035. The latest draft of the summit's cover decision suggested the final political outcome could be weaker than earlier proposals, amid resistance over money and fairness. Discussions around the second Global Stocktake (GST2) focused on fairness, science and finance, with developing countries pressing for credible means of implementation. Parallel commentary stressed that climate finance must move from pledges to action, especially for smallholders and vulnerable communities.
stories.whyItMatters: COP31 outcomes shape the future of the Paris Agreement's ratchet mechanism, climate finance flows and the pace of fossil fuel transition—core themes for GS-III environment and GS-II global governance.

static.topic: Supreme Court and Inter-State River Water Disputes

static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court's role in adjudicating disputes over sharing of inter-state rivers, including applications for interim relief and challenges to tribunal awards.
static.background: The Supreme Court is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; judicial review allows it to test laws and executive actions against the Constitution. stories.headline: As Trump courts Xi and Putin, middle powers chart their own course
stories.summary: President Donald Trump's parallel outreach to Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin has raised the prospect of a US–China–Russia trilateral engagement, with a reported 'Shenzhen pledge' on energy and fuel supplies and editorial calls for the three capitals to draw up a roadmap on nuclear weapons talks. The push is being watched for whether it moves beyond summit symbolism into substance on strategic stability and global energy markets. In parallel, middle powers — India among them — are described as hedging rather than aligning, deepening issue-based coalitions and regional partnerships of their own. Indian commentary reads the moment as an opening to build a 'fourth pole' and an Asian identity in which China participates without dominating, while cautioning that clubs such as the G20 and BRICS cannot substitute for the legitimacy of universal multilateral forums.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests India's strategic autonomy and multi-alignment at a moment of great-power churn, and feeds directly into GS-II questions on UN reform, minilateralism versus multilateralism, and nuclear arms control.

static.topic: United Nations and Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and UN Reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN, founded in 1945, has six principal organs. The Security Council has five permanent, veto-wielding members (the P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding member of the UN and among the largest contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping. The G4 — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — campaigns for Security Council expansion, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) process on reform remains inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: The reported US–China–Russia trilateral outreach, and the parallel hedging by middle powers, have renewed debate on whether a P5-centric order can deliver on nuclear risk reduction, energy security and climate finance — the core of India's case for a more representative Council.
static.wayForward: India can keep pressing for text-based negotiations in the IGN, build coalitions with African states around the Ezulwini Consensus, and use its G20 and BRICS platforms to show that reformed multilateralism delivers outcomes.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 elected for two-year terms.
The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague; UN headquarters is in New York.
The African Union was admitted as a permanent G20 member in 2023.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim to permanent membership rests on representativeness, population and peacekeeping contributions; assess the obstacles — veto politics, regional rivalries and the Ezulwini Consensus.

static.topic: India's Foreign Policy and Strategic Autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World; Bilateral, Regional and Global Groupings
static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment and the Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks, engaging simultaneously with the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954). Post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The Indo-Pacific concept and the Quad — with the US, Japan and Australia — gained salience after 2017.
static.whyInNews: As Washington courts Beijing and Moscow, Indian commentary argues for a distinct 'fourth pole' and an Asian identity in which China participates without dominating, with India as a bridge between the Global South, the West and Central Asia.
static.wayForward: Sustain issue-based coalitions, connectivity and energy partnerships while keeping universal forums central; avoid being drafted into any single bloc as great-power bargaining intensifies.
prelimsPointers: India assumed the G20 presidency in 2022–23.
India and Pakistan joined the SCO in 2017.
India is a member of both the Quad and BRICS.
static.mainsAngle: Balancing ties with the West, Russia and the Global South; evaluate India's role as a 'Voice of the Global South' and a bridging power.

static.topic: Nuclear Arms Control and Strategic Stability
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Nuclear Disarmament and Arms Control
static.whatIsIt: The global nuclear order rests on the NPT (1968, in force 1970), which recognises five nuclear-weapon states, and the CTBT (1996), which has not entered into force because key Annex 2 states have not ratified. Bilateral US–Russia treaties have been the main vehicle for warhead reductions.
static.background: The NPT was extended indefinitely in 1995. The CTBT was adopted in 1996 but remains unratified by several Annex 2 states. New START (2010) was extended in 2021 for five years; the absence of a successor arrangement has renewed focus on strategic stability and on the role of China's expanding arsenal.
static.whyInNews: Editorial commentary on the reported US–China–Russia trilateral engagement argues the three capitals must draw up a roadmap for nuclear weapons talks rather than settle for a summit photo-op.
static.wayForward: Revive structured dialogue among the largest arsenals, keep risk-reduction and crisis-communication channels open, and ensure any new framework does not erode the NPT's universality or ignore the legitimate security interests of non-nuclear-weapon states.
prelimsPointers: The NPT recognises five nuclear-weapon states: the US, Russia, China, France and the UK.
India is not a party to the NPT or the CTBT.
The CTBT has not entered into force; the IAEA is based in Vienna.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether plurilateral great-power arms control can substitute for universal instruments, and what it implies for India's No First Use doctrine and credible minimum deterrence.

prelims: The reported trilateral engagement is between the US, China and Russia; the 'Shenzhen pledge' is linked to cooperation on global fuel and energy supplies.
Middle powers — including India, Brazil, Turkey and Gulf and ASEAN states — are described as pursuing issue-based coalitions rather than bloc alignment.
India is not a party to the NPT or the CTBT and maintains a No First Use nuclear doctrine; it is a member of both BRICS and the Quad.
The African Union was admitted as a permanent G20 member in 2023; India held the G20 presidency in 2022–23.
stories.mainsQuestion: The return of great-power condominium politics is coinciding with a crisis of legitimacy in multilateral institutions. In this context, examine how India can pursue strategic autonomy and build a 'fourth pole' without weakening the rules-based multilateral order.

stories.headline: ICJ Myanmar ruling revives Rohingya genocide accountability questions
stories.summary: An ICJ ruling in the case concerning Myanmar's treatment of the Rohingya has revived questions about genocide accountability and the enforcement of international law. The Indian Express argues in an editorial that the ICJ verdict alone is not enough and that broader state and institutional action is needed. The case remains a test of the Genocide Convention and the limits of international judicial remedies.

static.topic: Indian Supreme Court and Rohingya-related litigation
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court is India's apex court under Article 124, with writ jurisdiction under Article 32 and power of judicial review. It has heard petitions concerning Rohingya refugees, deportation and refugee rights.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Article 32 (SC) and 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction.
static.socioEconomic: India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention; Rohingya refugees face deportation and detention, raising humanitarian and security debates.
static.whyInNews: The ICJ ruling has revived questions about the Indian Supreme Court's role in Rohingya deportation and refugee protection cases.
static.wayForward: A clear domestic refugee law and consistent judicial standards could reconcile security concerns with non-refoulement and human rights obligations.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction: disputes between Centre and states (Art. 131).
Advisory jurisdiction under Article 143.
Article 32 provides constitutional remedies for fundamental rights.

static.topic: ICJ, UN and enforcement of international law
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the UN, settling disputes between states and giving advisory opinions. The UN Security Council has primary responsibility for maintaining peace and security.
static.background: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 campaigns for UNSC expansion.
static.geography: ICJ sits in The Hague, Netherlands; UN HQ in New York.
static.whyInNews: The ICJ's Myanmar ruling highlights the limits of international judicial remedies when enforcement depends on the UNSC and member states.
static.wayForward: Strengthen multilateral mechanisms, including UNSC action and universal jurisdiction, to ensure compliance with ICJ orders and the Genocide Convention.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for 2-year terms.
ICJ is in The Hague; UN HQ in New York.
ICJ hears disputes between states, not individuals.

static.topic: Genocide Convention and The Gambia v Myanmar
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Law
static.whatIsIt: The 1948 Genocide Convention criminalises genocide and obliges states to prevent and punish it. The Gambia filed a case against Myanmar at the ICJ in 2019 alleging violations against the Rohingya.
static.background: The ICJ ordered provisional measures in January 2020 directing Myanmar to prevent genocide and preserve evidence. In July 2022, the ICJ rejected Myanmar's preliminary objections and affirmed its jurisdiction.
static.geography: Myanmar; The Gambia; ICJ in The Hague.
static.socioEconomic: Rohingya displacement to Bangladesh and elsewhere created a major humanitarian crisis.
static.whyInNews: The ICJ's ruling revives accountability questions and tests the Genocide Convention's enforcement.
static.wayForward: States should support the case, comply with ICJ orders, and address impunity through international and domestic mechanisms.

ICJ provisional measures are binding but enforcement is political.

static.whatIsIt: A mission to secure India's supply of critical minerals and materials through exploration, mining, processing, recycling and overseas acquisition.
static.background: Announced in the Union Budget 2025-26 to reduce import dependence for minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and rare earths. It builds on earlier steps like the 2023 amendment to the MMDR Act, the release of a critical minerals list, and KABIL's overseas asset acquisitions.

static.socioEconomic: Critical minerals are inputs for EVs, renewable energy, defence, electronics and semiconductors; supply security affects manufacturing jobs, energy transition and strategic autonomy.

static.wayForward: Strengthen exploration, processing and recycling; promote public-private partnerships; secure overseas mineral assets; build strategic stockpiles; align with environmental and community safeguards.

static.topic: Critical Minerals and India's Resource Security

static.whatIsIt: Critical minerals are non-fuel minerals essential for modern technologies, clean energy, defence and electronics, whose supply chains are vulnerable to geopolitical and market disruptions.
static.background: India has historically focused on bulk minerals like coal and iron ore. Rising demand for EVs, solar panels, wind turbines and semiconductors has exposed dependence on imports, especially from China. Policy responses include the 2023 MMDR Amendment, critical minerals list, KABIL, and the National Critical Mineral Mission.

static.socioEconomic: Affects manufacturing competitiveness, energy transition costs, national security and employment in sunrise sectors.
static.whyInNews: The Hindu opinion argues India's minerals policy must move from extraction targets to 'material security'.
static.wayForward: Invest in domestic processing and recycling, diversify imports, secure overseas mines, build strategic reserves, and promote research in mineral substitutes.
prelimsPointers: Critical minerals are essential for electric vehicles, renewable energy, defence and electronics.
India is heavily import-dependent for lithium, cobalt, nickel and rare earths.
The MMDR Amendment Act, 2023 enabled the auction of critical mineral blocks.

static.topic: Crude Oil Production and India's Energy Security
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Infrastructure: Energy; Energy security; Import dependence
static.whatIsIt: Crude oil is a key primary energy source; India's domestic production is limited relative to its refining and consumption demand.
static.background: India imports over 85% of its crude oil requirement. Major domestic fields include Mumbai High, Rajasthan and Krishna-Godavari basin. Production has stagnated or declined in recent years, while demand has risen with economic growth.
static.geography: Major oil-producing regions: Mumbai Offshore, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Assam and Krishna-Godavari basin; imports from West Asia, Africa, Russia and the Americas.
static.socioEconomic: High import dependence affects the current account deficit, inflation, fiscal revenue and energy affordability; also shapes India's foreign policy and strategic petroleum reserves.
static.whyInNews: TheWire.in reports that India's crude oil production is likely to fall by 20% over the next decade even as demand continues to increase.
static.wayForward: Boost upstream investment, enhanced oil recovery, diversify import sources, expand strategic petroleum reserves, and accelerate ethanol blending, EVs and renewables to reduce oil intensity.
prelimsPointers: India imports more than 85% of its crude oil requirement.

static.topic: Riemann Hypothesis and the Millennium Prize Problems
static.syllabusNode: Science and Technology — developments and their applications; basic mathematics of prime numbers
static.whatIsIt: The Riemann hypothesis, stated by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, conjectures that all non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2. It governs the distribution of prime numbers and underpins large parts of analytic number theory.
static.background: Proposed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859. The Clay Mathematics Institute listed it in 2000 among seven Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a US$1 million prize. Only the Poincaré conjecture has been resolved — by Grigori Perelman (2002–03), who declined the prize in 2010. The hypothesis has been checked computationally over very large ranges of zeros, but no proof exists.
static.socioEconomic: The hardness of prime-number problems underpins RSA and other public-key cryptosystems; a proof would not break encryption but would deepen understanding of the number-theoretic assumptions on which digital security rests.
static.whyInNews: An Anthropic mathematician claims Claude helped produce a proof of the hypothesis; independent verification is pending.
static.wayForward: Any such claim must clear independent refereeing and, increasingly, machine-checkable formal verification (proof assistants such as Lean or Coq) before acceptance; AI-assisted mathematics should meet the same peer-review standard as human work.
prelimsPointers: The Riemann hypothesis was stated in 1859 and concerns the distribution of prime numbers.
It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems announced by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000.
Only the Poincaré conjecture among them has been solved — by Grigori Perelman.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how AI tools are changing the practice of mathematical research and the standards by which proof and verification are judged.

static.topic: India's AI Governance Framework
static.syllabusNode: Awareness in the fields of IT, computers and technology; government policies and interventions
static.whatIsIt: The institutional and legal architecture for artificial intelligence in India: NITI Aayog's National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (2018), the IndiaAI Mission (2024), the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and MeitY advisories on AI model deployment.
static.background: NITI Aayog's 2018 strategy identified AI for inclusive growth as a priority. The IndiaAI Mission was approved in March 2024 with an outlay of about ₹10,372 crore, covering compute, datasets, application development and skilling. MeitY issued advisories on AI model deployment in 2024, and the DPDP Act, 2023 supplies the data-governance backbone. Globally, the EU AI Act (2024) is the first comprehensive, risk-based AI statute.
static.socioEconomic: Access to compute, data localisation and skilling determine whether Indian firms can compete; the 'multi-trillion dollar arms race' framing points to global flows of AI capital and talent.
static.whyInNews: Anthropic's reported IPO and the wider AI arms-race debate raise questions about India's regulatory posture and investment strategy.
static.wayForward: Move from advisory circulars towards a risk-based statutory framework, expand public compute under the IndiaAI Mission, and build domestic evaluation, safety and skilling capacity.
prelimsPointers: The IndiaAI Mission was approved in March 2024 with an outlay of about ₹10,372 crore.
The DPDP Act, 2023 is India's first comprehensive data-protection statute.
The EU AI Act (2024) follows a risk-based, tiered regulatory approach.
static.mainsAngle: Should India regulate AI through statute or rely on self-regulation? Discuss with reference to innovation, safety and strategic autonomy.

static.topic: Right to Privacy and On-Screen Data Accessed by AI Agents
static.syllabusNode: Fundamental Rights — right to privacy; government policies on information technology
static.whatIsIt: The constitutional right to privacy read into Article 21, together with the statutory protections governing personal data and the on-screen information that operating-system-level AI agents can access.
static.background: In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a nine-judge bench unanimously held privacy to be a fundamental right. The IT Act, 2000 (Sections 43A and 72) and the SPDI Rules, 2011 preceded the DPDP Act, 2023, which introduced consent and purpose-limitation obligations for digital personal data.
static.socioEconomic: Operating-system-level AI assistants blur the boundary between device and app, shifting de facto control over user data towards platform and OS vendors.
static.whyInNews: Signal blocked screenshots on its app to stop OS-level AI agents from reading private chats.
static.wayForward: Enforce purpose limitation and data minimisation on AI agents, mandate clear consent and auditability, and align DPDP rules with platform-level access controls.
prelimsPointers: The right to privacy was recognised as a fundamental right in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017).
The DPDP Act, 2023 governs the processing of digital personal data in India.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how AI agents that read on-screen content challenge existing privacy safeguards, and suggest appropriate regulatory responses.

prelims: The Riemann hypothesis, stated by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.
Anthropic is the developer of the Claude family of AI models; a company mathematician claims Claude assisted in a proof of the hypothesis.

stories.mainsQuestion: AI systems are increasingly credited with advances in fundamental science even as their outputs remain difficult to verify. Examine the implications for the standards of scientific proof and for India's AI research and governance strategy.

Analysts frame the crisis as a test of China's expanding diplomatic and economic role in the Middle East, while Gulf states simultaneously push ahead with their own trade-integration agenda.

The crisis also tests the credibility of US-led security guarantees and the reach of China's mediating role — core GS-II themes.

static.background: Houthi forces took Sanaa in 2014; the Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 at the Yemeni government's request. The 2018 UN-brokered Stockholm Agreement sought a ceasefire around Hodeidah port, a lifeline for humanitarian imports. The war has produced one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
static.geography: Yemen sits at the southern mouth of the Red Sea, commanding the Bab-el-Mandeb strait; Hodeidah is a Red Sea port and Yemen's principal entry point for food and fuel.
static.socioEconomic: Prolonged conflict has collapsed basic services and left most of the population dependent on aid; attacks on Red Sea shipping raise insurance and freight costs for global trade.
static.whyInNews: The Saudi-led coalition said it targeted Hodeidah port capabilities used for weapons smuggling, while Saudi Arabia reported intercepting three Houthi missiles aimed at Riyadh.

static.topic: Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Regional Trade Integration
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Regional Organisations / India & West Asia
static.whatIsIt: The GCC is a six-member political and economic union of Gulf monarchies — Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE — with a customs union and a common market.
static.background: Founded in 1981 with its secretariat in Riyadh. A customs union took effect in 2003 and a common market was launched in 2008; plans for a single currency stalled after Oman and the UAE opted out.
static.geography: Member states sit on the Persian Gulf and the Arabian Peninsula, controlling the Strait of Hormuz and holding a large share of world hydrocarbon reserves.
static.socioEconomic: GCC economies remain hydrocarbon-dependent and pursue diversification visions; intra-GCC trade is limited by non-tariff barriers, differing standards and sovereignty concerns.
static.whyInNews: A commentary examines the GCC's persistent difficulty in deepening trade integration even as the region absorbs fresh security shocks.
static.wayForward: Harmonising standards and customs procedures, deepening the common market, and pursuing trade and investment agreements with partners such as India.
prelimsPointers: The GCC has six members, was founded in 1981 and is headquartered in Riyadh.
The GCC customs union came into effect in 2003; the common market was launched in 2008.

static.topic: India's Foreign Policy & Strategic Autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India & the World
static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and the Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks, engaging simultaneously across the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954). Post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The Indo-Pacific concept and the Quad (with the US, Japan and Australia) gained salience after 2017.
static.socioEconomic: West Asia hosts a large Indian diaspora and supplies a major share of India's crude oil and natural gas; Gulf remittances are a significant source of foreign exchange.
static.whyInNews: Escalation involving Iran, the US and Gulf actors, plus Red Sea disruption, tests India's balancing act between energy suppliers, diaspora hosts and Western partners.
static.wayForward: Sustained multi-alignment, contingency planning for energy supply and shipping routes, and active diplomacy urging de-escalation.

India and Pakistan joined the SCO in 2017.

stories.headline: Cyclone Akvan catches Odisha off guard; Karnataka HC orders forest mapping
stories.summary: Cyclone Akvan developed unexpectedly and surprised forecasters tracking the Odisha coast, reviving questions about cyclone prediction and east-coast preparedness. In Karnataka, the High Court directed the state government to identify and record forests and forest-like areas, a step tied to the long-standing legal ambiguity over 'deemed forests' under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. In West Bengal, the release of tigress T138 in Buxa Tiger Reserve has been welcomed as a conservation milestone but triggered protests from forest villagers against tourism curbs imposed to reduce disturbance. A separate feature traces India's black leopards, using melanism as a lens on habitat pressure outside protected areas.
stories.whyItMatters: The three strands converge on a single exam theme: conservation outcomes in India depend as much on administrative record-keeping, forecasting capacity and community consent as on statutory protection. Forest identification, translocation protocols and cyclone preparedness are recurring GS-III and GS-I hooks.

perspectives.take: Frames the High Court order as a judicial push to make Karnataka's forest record legally complete, foregrounding administrative delay over conservation outcomes.
Reads Cyclone Akvan as a climate-signal story — an unexpectedly intensifying system exposing the limits of forecasting and coastal preparedness.
Centres the conservation-versus-livelihood tension, giving forest villagers' grievances over tourism curbs weight alongside the translocation's success.

static.topic: Biodiversity, Wetlands & Conservation
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Biodiversity & Conservation
static.whatIsIt: India's legal and policy architecture for protecting forests, wildlife and biodiversity, anchored in the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, the Biological Diversity Act 2002 and commitments under the Convention on Biological Diversity.
static.background: In T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (1996), the Supreme Court read 'forest' in its dictionary sense to cover 'forest-like areas' irrespective of ownership or notification, creating the category of 'deemed forests'. The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 was amended in 2023 to narrow its application to notified forests and land recorded as forest on or after 25 October 1980, intensifying litigation over unrecorded forests. India is one of 17 megadiverse countries and a party to the CBD (1992) and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022).
static.geography: Karnataka's Western Ghats and Malnad belt hold dense evergreen and semi-evergreen forests; Buxa Tiger Reserve lies in West Bengal's Alipurduar district in the Eastern Himalaya, contiguous with forested areas of Bhutan.
static.socioEconomic: Forest-dwelling communities depend on tourism, non-timber forest produce and wage labour; conservation restrictions interact with rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006, and can sharpen human-wildlife conflict.
static.whyInNews: The Karnataka High Court has directed the state government to identify forests and forest-like areas, while the translocation of tigress T138 to Buxa Tiger Reserve has prompted protests by forest villagers against tourism curbs.
static.wayForward: Complete state-level records of forest-like areas transparently, reconcile them with Forest Rights Act claims and village forest rights, and design tourism and translocation protocols with community consent and benefit-sharing.
prelimsPointers: India's four biodiversity hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats–Sri Lanka and Sundaland/Nicobar.
Forests and protection of wild animals and birds are Concurrent List subjects after the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
World Wetlands Day is observed on 2 February.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how judicial direction and statutory ambiguity over 'deemed forests' shape conservation outcomes and the rights of forest-dwelling communities.

static.topic: Indian Monsoon & Physical Geography
static.syllabusNode: Geography — Physical Geography of India
static.whatIsIt: The monsoon system and the physical processes that generate tropical cyclones over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea.
static.background: Tropical cyclones form over warm ocean waters with low vertical wind shear and sufficient Coriolis force away from the equator; India's east coast is more cyclone-prone than the west, and the IMD is the regional specialised meteorological centre for the North Indian Ocean. The monsoon delivers roughly 75% of annual rainfall between June and September, modulated by El Niño/La Niña and the Indian Ocean Dipole.
static.geography: Odisha's coastline faces the Bay of Bengal, where cyclones are frequent; the Eastern Ghats and the deltaic plains of the Mahanadi-Brahmani systems channel storm surge and flooding.
static.socioEconomic: Dense coastal populations, agriculture, fisheries and infrastructure in Odisha and neighbouring states are exposed to wind damage, storm surge, saline intrusion and flooding.
static.whyInNews: Cyclone Akvan developed unexpectedly and surprised forecasters monitoring Odisha, reviving questions about cyclone prediction and east-coast preparedness.
static.wayForward: Strengthen rapid-update forecasting, last-mile warning dissemination, cyclone shelters and multi-hazard resilience planning that accounts for climate-driven intensification.
prelimsPointers: Himalayan rivers are perennial (snow-fed); peninsular rivers are largely seasonal and rain-fed.
El Niño generally weakens the Indian monsoon while La Niña tends to strengthen it; the IOD also modulates rainfall.
The IMD is the WMO-designated regional specialised meteorological centre for the North Indian Ocean.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how climate change is altering cyclone frequency, intensity and track predictability, and evaluate India's coastal disaster preparedness.

static.topic: Federalism & Centre-State Relations
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: The division of legislative and administrative powers between the Union and states under the Seventh Schedule, and the institutional mechanisms that manage the relationship.
static.background: The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved forests and wildlife protection from the State List to the Concurrent List. The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2007) reviewed Centre-state balance, while the Governor (Article 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a recurring flashpoint over assent to Bills.
static.socioEconomic: Forest and land governance sits at the intersection of state revenue and forest departments, central conservation law and local community rights, so coordination failures carry direct livelihood costs.
static.whyInNews: The Karnataka High Court's direction to the state government to identify forests and forest-like areas illustrates judicial enforcement of a Concurrent List obligation and the Centre-state coordination it requires.
static.wayForward: Use intergovernmental forums and model frameworks to standardise forest record-keeping, while respecting state capacity and the constitutional division of powers.
prelimsPointers: Forests and protection of wild animals and birds are Concurrent List subjects, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
On repugnancy in the Concurrent List, union law prevails unless the state law has been reserved for and received the President's assent (Article 254).
The Inter-State Council (Article 263) is a recommendatory body for inter-state coordination.
static.mainsAngle: How far does judicial intervention help resolve coordination gaps between the Union and states in environmental governance? Examine with examples.

prelims: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (1996) expanded the meaning of 'forest' to include 'forest-like areas' irrespective of ownership or notification.
The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 was amended in 2023 to cover only notified forests and land recorded as forest on or after 25 October 1980.
Buxa Tiger Reserve, notified in 1983, lies in Alipurduar district, West Bengal, and is contiguous with forested areas in Bhutan.
Melanism in leopards is a genetic condition causing excess dark pigmentation; it is reported mainly from the Western Ghats and parts of eastern India.
stories.mainsQuestion: Conservation in India increasingly depends on judicial direction rather than statutory clarity. Critically examine this proposition in the light of forest identification drives, tiger translocation and the rights of forest-dwelling communities.

static.topic: India's Foreign Exchange Reserves and External Sector Buffers
static.syllabusNode: Economy — External Sector: Balance of Payments and Forex Reserves
static.whatIsIt: Forex reserves are the external assets held and managed by the RBI, comprising Foreign Currency Assets, gold, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) and the Reserve Tranche Position with the IMF. They cushion balance-of-payments shocks, support the rupee and signal external sector credibility.
static.background: India's reserves were critically low during the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis, when gold had to be pledged abroad. Sustained accumulation followed liberalisation, export growth and capital inflows, and reserves crossed the $700-billion mark in 2024. The RBI publishes reserve data on a weekly basis, and movements are driven by both transactions and valuation (revaluation) effects.
static.socioEconomic: Adequate reserves lower the cost of external borrowing, stabilise the rupee and reduce exchange-rate volatility for importers and exporters. Holding large reserves, however, carries a sterilisation cost and can complicate domestic liquidity management.
static.whyInNews: Reserves declined by $14.21 billion to $705.34 billion, with the fall attributed to revaluation rather than a capital outflow.
static.wayForward: Maintain a comfortable import cover, diversify the currency composition of reserves, deepen local-currency trade settlement and monitor valuation risk from gold and global bond holdings.
prelimsPointers: Forex reserves = Foreign Currency Assets + gold + SDRs + Reserve Tranche Position with the IMF.
The RBI releases weekly data on India's foreign exchange reserves.
Import cover (months of imports a reserve stock can finance) is a standard adequacy metric.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether the size and composition of India's forex reserves are adequate to absorb external shocks in a period of volatile commodity prices and capital flows.

static.topic: Gold Prices, Gold Imports and the Current Account Deficit
static.syllabusNode: Economy — External Sector: Current Account Deficit and Commodity Markets
static.whatIsIt: Gold functions as a global safe-haven asset and, in India, as a major household store of value. Because India is among the world's largest importers and consumers of gold, its price and import volumes feed directly into the trade deficit, the current account deficit and the rupee.
static.background: Gold imports were liberalised after the 1991 reforms. To curb the import bill, the government launched the Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme and the Gold Monetisation Scheme in 2015, and has periodically adjusted import duties. Gold also forms a component of India's official foreign exchange reserves.
static.socioEconomic: Gold demand is tied to weddings, festivals and rural incomes, making it a savings instrument as well as a consumption good. Sharp price corrections affect household wealth, jewellers' inventories and the import bill.
static.whyInNews: Gold prices have fallen by about 25% over nine months, raising the question of whether the correction could extend further.
static.wayForward: Channel household savings towards financial instruments, strengthen gold monetisation and recycling, and monitor the import bill's impact on the current account.
prelimsPointers: India is among the largest importers and consumers of gold in the world.
Gold held by the RBI is a component of the country's foreign exchange reserves.
Sovereign Gold Bonds and the Gold Monetisation Scheme were introduced in 2015 to reduce physical gold imports.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how gold imports influence India's external balance and evaluate the effectiveness of policy instruments designed to reduce the gold import bill.

static.topic: State Borrowing Limits and Fiscal Federalism (Article 293)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism: Centre-State Financial Relations
static.whatIsIt: Article 293 of the Constitution governs borrowing by states. Under Article 293(3), a state that has outstanding loans from the Centre requires the Centre's consent to borrow further. States additionally self-limit borrowing through their own Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) legislation.
static.background: The Centre enacted the FRBM Act in 2003, and states followed with their own FRBM laws. Fiscal deficit norms for states have generally been anchored around 3% of GSDP, with conditional additional space tied to reforms such as the power sector. During the pandemic, the Centre permitted extra borrowing linked to specified reform conditions.
static.geography: Uttarakhand is a Himalayan state with a hill economy, a limited industrial base and relatively high dependence on central transfers.
static.socioEconomic: Borrowing caps directly constrain state capital expenditure on infrastructure, health and education. Off-budget borrowings by state entities have been a recurring concern for fiscal transparency.
static.whyInNews: Uttarakhand's Chief Minister met the Prime Minister seeking relief for the state from the Centre's borrowing cap.
static.wayForward: Move towards a predictable, rule-based borrowing framework, strengthen state FRBM compliance and transparency on off-budget liabilities, and expand states' own tax capacity.
prelimsPointers: Under Article 293(3), a state with outstanding loans from the Centre needs the Centre's consent to borrow.
The FRBM Act, 2003 provides the statutory framework for fiscal deficit targets.
State fiscal deficit norms are commonly expressed as a percentage of GSDP.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether conditional caps on state borrowing strengthen fiscal discipline or undermine cooperative fiscal federalism.

prelims: India's forex reserves comprise Foreign Currency Assets, gold, SDRs and the Reserve Tranche Position, and are reported weekly by the RBI.
Article 293(3) requires a state with outstanding central loans to obtain the Centre's consent before borrowing further.
SEBI is the statutory regulator of India's securities market, established under the SEBI Act, 1992.
Gold held by the RBI is counted within the country's official foreign exchange reserves.
stories.mainsQuestion: India's external sector buffers have come under valuation pressure even as gold prices correct sharply. Examine the implications of these movements for the current account and macroeconomic stability, and suggest measures to strengthen external resilience.

stories.headline: Supreme Court allows bike taxis, strikes down UP service-exclusion rules
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on 20 November 2026 delivered a clutch of orders spanning transport regulation, service law and its own administrative functioning. It dismissed the Karnataka government's appeal seeking to revive its ban on bike taxis, holding that the better course is to regulate the service rather than prohibit it. In a separate matter, the Court struck down Uttar Pradesh statutory provisions that excluded work-charged employees' pre-regularisation service from being counted, restoring the position that such service counts for the employees concerned. The Court also directed an inquiry into why its own Registry had failed to list an Enforcement Directorate plea challenging bail for more than three years. Together the orders reaffirm judicial review over state action while turning a spotlight on internal court administration.
stories.whyItMatters: Covers judicial review of state regulatory and service-law action, the regulation-versus-prohibition debate for aggregator transport, and judicial administration — recurring GS-II themes on the judiciary and federalism.

perspectives.take: Frames the outcome as a clean win for bike-taxi operators, headlining the Court's rejection of Karnataka's bid to restore the ban.

static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts & Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary (Supreme Court, Judicial Review, Court Administration)
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Art. 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Art. 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction.
static.whyInNews: The Court dismissed Karnataka's plea to restore a bike-taxi ban, struck down UP provisions excluding work-charged employees' pre-regularisation service from being counted, and ordered a probe into its Registry's failure to list an ED plea against bail for over three years.
static.wayForward: Tackle pendency and Registry-level delays through case-management and listing reforms, and fill judicial vacancies; internal administrative accountability is as important as independence.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction: disputes between the Centre and states (Art. 131); advisory jurisdiction under Article 143.
Appellate powers run through Articles 132–136, with Article 136 conferring special leave to appeal; Article 142 allows the Court to do complete justice.
static.mainsAngle: Examine judicial backlog, vacancies and pendency; the balance between judicial independence and accountability.

static.topic: Federalism & Centre-State Relations
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution (Seventh Schedule, State Regulatory Autonomy)
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union: powers are divided between the Union and States via the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule), with residuary powers with the Union (Art. 248).
static.background: Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions examined the Centre-State balance. The Governor (Art. 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a flashpoint over assent to Bills (Art. 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Art. 201).
static.geography: Transport regulation operates through state RTO machinery under a central statute, making it a working example of shared Union-State competence.
static.socioEconomic: Bike taxis are a first-and-last-mile mobility option in cities and a livelihood for a large pool of drivers; blanket bans affect both commuters and driver earnings, which is why the Court preferred regulation.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court declined to restore Karnataka's ban on bike taxis, framing the issue as one of regulation rather than prohibition — a reminder that transport regulation is shared between the Union and the states.
static.wayForward: States should frame aggregator and contract-carriage rules with clear licensing, safety, insurance and fare norms instead of blanket bans, so that regulatory power is exercised proportionately.
prelimsPointers: Concurrent List: union law prevails on repugnancy unless the state law is reserved for the President's assent (Art. 254).
Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
Motor vehicles, including mechanically propelled vehicles, fall in the Concurrent List (Entry 35); the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 is the central framework implemented by states.
static.mainsAngle: Recent spats over the Governor's assent and fiscal devolution — assess cooperative federalism in practice, including in shared-competence sectors like transport.

prelims: Supreme Court: Article 124 (establishment); appellate powers under Articles 132–136; special leave under Article 136; power to do complete justice under Article 142.
Judicial review is exercised through writ jurisdiction under Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Courts).
Motor vehicles, including mechanically propelled vehicles, are a Concurrent List subject (Entry 35); the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 is implemented by states through RTO rules.
Work-charged employees are engaged on a temporary/work basis and regularised later; whether pre-regularisation service counts is a question of service jurisprudence.
stories.mainsQuestion: The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that regulation, not prohibition, is the appropriate response to new service models. Examine this proposition in the light of the Court's bike-taxi ruling and the wider debate on state regulatory autonomy and judicial review.

stories.headline: Justice Verma Resigns, Tells Parliament Impeachment Proceedings Now Infructuous
stories.summary: Justice Yashwant Verma, who was facing a removal motion in Parliament, has resigned and has written to Parliament contending that the impeachment proceedings against him have become infructuous. The motion had been admitted and referred to a statutory inquiry committee under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, an enactment that is silent on the effect of a judge's resignation while the process is pending. The development has revived the debate on whether resignation can be used to short-circuit a constitutionally mandated accountability process. In a parallel courtroom development, the Supreme Court issued notice to an advocate over remarks against the Chief Justice, invoking its contempt jurisdiction to protect the dignity of the office. Separately, TheWire.in examined how the Comptroller and Auditor General is chosen, extending the debate on the independence of constitutional offices.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the constitutional design of judicial removal under Articles 124(4) and 217 and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, and the perennial GS-II tension between judicial independence and judicial accountability.

static.topic: Removal of Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Independence and Accountability of the Higher Judiciary
static.whatIsIt: A judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court can be removed only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by a motion passed by a special majority in each House of Parliament and an order of the President (Articles 124(4) and 124(5); Article 217(1)(b) for High Court judges). The inquiry procedure is laid down in the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 and the Judges (Inquiry) Rules, 1969.
static.background: The high removal threshold was deliberately written into the Constitution to insulate judges from political pressure. The Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 gave the process a statutory shape. The only motion that has ever reached the inquiry-committee stage was against Justice V. Ramaswami (1993), and it failed in the Lok Sabha. A separate in-house procedure (1999, revised 2014) handles complaints that do not amount to grounds for removal.
static.whyInNews: Justice Yashwant Verma, facing a removal motion, resigned and told Parliament that the impeachment proceedings had become infructuous, raising the unresolved question of what happens to a pending motion when the judge quits.
static.wayForward: Clarify through statute or rules whether a removal motion abates on resignation, and strengthen the in-house complaint mechanism so that serious allegations are examined even if the judge resigns.
prelimsPointers: Removal requires a special majority in each House — a majority of the total membership plus two-thirds of members present and voting — followed by a Presidential order.
A motion needs the support of 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members to be admitted by the presiding officer.
No judge has ever been removed by impeachment in India.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether resignation during removal proceedings defeats the purpose of the accountability mechanism, and suggest safeguards that preserve both judicial independence and public confidence.

static.topic: Parliament's Role in the Removal of Judges
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament and the Legislative Process: Motions, Committees and Accountability
static.whatIsIt: Parliament is the sole forum for removing a judge. Once a motion is admitted, the presiding officer constitutes a three-member committee — a Supreme Court judge, a High Court Chief Justice and a distinguished jurist — which inquires into the charges and submits a report; the House then votes on the motion.
static.background: The Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 and the Judges (Inquiry) Rules, 1969 govern the committee stage. The Act is silent on the consequences of a judge's resignation or retirement while the motion is pending, and parliamentary practice offers no precedent, since no removal motion has ever been carried.
static.whyInNews: Justice Verma's letter to Parliament arguing that the proceedings are infructuous after his resignation has put the parliamentary procedure for removal of judges in the spotlight.
static.wayForward: Parliament could codify the effect of resignation, retirement or superannuation on a pending motion, and lay down timelines for the inquiry committee's report.
prelimsPointers: The inquiry committee under the 1968 Act has three members: one Supreme Court judge, one High Court Chief Justice and one distinguished jurist.
A removal motion can be introduced in either House of Parliament.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether Parliament's removal procedure for judges needs statutory reform to deal with resignation, delay and the absence of any precedent of a successful motion.

static.topic: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Constitutional Bodies: Comptroller and Auditor General
static.whatIsIt: Article 148 provides for a CAG appointed by the President, who audits the accounts of the Union and the states and controls the issue of money from the Consolidated Fund; duties and powers are detailed in the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971.
static.background: The office descends from the pre-independence Auditor General. The Constitution gave it security of tenure — removal only on the same grounds and in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge — and charged its salary on the Consolidated Fund of India. The appointment itself remains an executive decision, and proposals for a broad-based selection committee have been made, on the lines of the model adopted for Election Commissioners in 2023.
static.socioEconomic: Audit reports feed the Public Accounts Committee and shape public debate on fiscal transparency and the quality of public expenditure.
static.whyInNews: TheWire.in's piece 'Who Chooses the Nation's Auditor?' revives the debate on how the CAG is selected and whether executive discretion in the appointment undercuts audit independence.
static.wayForward: Consider a transparent, broad-based selection process with published criteria, while retaining the CAG's security of tenure and financial independence.
prelimsPointers: The CAG is appointed by the President and can be removed only in the manner of a Supreme Court judge.
A former CAG is not eligible for any further office under the Government of India or a state.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether the appointment process of the CAG affects the independence of audit in India, and examine the case for a statutory selection committee.

prelims: A judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court can be removed only on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by a special-majority motion in Parliament (Articles 124(4) and 217).
The Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 governs the inquiry but does not expressly state what happens if the judge resigns while the motion is pending.
No judge has been removed in India; the motion against Justice V. Ramaswami (1993) failed in the Lok Sabha.
The Supreme Court can initiate contempt proceedings for remarks that scandalise the court or lower the authority of the Chief Justice.
stories.mainsQuestion: Resignation of a judge midway through removal proceedings raises questions about the efficacy of India's judicial accountability framework. Examine the constitutional and statutory provisions for the removal of judges and suggest reforms that make the process credible without compromising judicial independence.

static.topic: Semiconductor Manufacturing and the India Semiconductor Mission
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Industry, Infrastructure and Investment Models
static.whatIsIt: Semiconductors are the foundational input for electronics, defence, automotive and computing hardware. India's national push runs through the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, which offers fiscal support to fabrication (fab), ATMP/OSAT and display units. States layer their own incentives — capital subsidy, subsidised land, power and water — on top to attract projects.
static.background: The ISM was launched in 2021 with an outlay of about ₹76,000 crore, alongside a Design Linked Incentive scheme and the Chips to Startup programme. Approved projects include an ATMP facility in Gujarat and fab/OSAT units in Gujarat and Assam. States including Gujarat, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Assam and Andhra Pradesh have announced semiconductor or electronics policies to compete for investment.
static.geography: Fabs are water- and power-intensive, so site selection hinges on assured utilities, land parcels and port/air links; Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are among the states actively bidding.
static.socioEconomic: Semiconductor units create relatively small but high-skill, high-wage employment with large multiplier effects on supplier ecosystems; the risk is a subsidy race that transfers fiscal resources without changing underlying locational economics.
static.whyInNews: Andhra Pradesh has raised its semiconductor incentives, offering up to 80% support for silicon fabs, intensifying inter-state competition for fab investment.
static.wayForward: Shift from pure subsidy competition to ecosystem building — design talent, water and power assurance, testing and packaging clusters, critical-mineral and chemical supply chains — and consider a coordinated national framework so states do not bid away fiscal space.
prelimsPointers: The India Semiconductor Mission operates under MeitY with an outlay of about ₹76,000 crore.
Fabrication units are capital-intensive and require large, reliable supplies of water and electricity.
State incentive packages typically combine capital subsidy with land, power tariff and stamp-duty concessions.
static.mainsAngle: Inter-state subsidy competition to attract high-technology manufacturing can distort locational choices and strain state finances — examine in the context of India's semiconductor mission and suggest how cooperative federalism can make incentives more efficient.

static.topic: Public Procurement and Tender Reform
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Transparency, Accountability and Institutional Reform
static.whatIsIt: Public procurement covers government purchase of goods, works and services, governed centrally by the General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017 and by state procurement manuals, with the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) as the national online platform. Award is conventionally made to the lowest responsive bidder (L1), which can produce abnormally low bids that later fail on execution.
static.background: GFR 2017 consolidated central procurement rules; GeM was launched in 2016 to bring transparency and speed to routine purchases. Repeated attempts to enact a dedicated national public procurement law have not fructified, leaving a patchwork of rules across the Union and states. Quality-cum-cost-based selection (QCBS) and two-envelope systems are used in some sectors to balance price with capability.
static.socioEconomic: Abnormally low bids can translate into stalled projects, cost overruns, litigation, poor asset quality and stressed contractors, ultimately raising the true cost of public infrastructure to citizens.
static.whyInNews: The Centre is reported to be moving to scrutinise rock-bottom bids in government tenders, covering both large infrastructure projects and procurement of goods and services, to prevent contractors from winning at steep discounts and then struggling with execution.
static.wayForward: Strengthen pre-qualification and bid-capacity assessment, use price-reasonableness checks and QCBS where quality matters, mandate timely payments and dispute resolution, and publish tender outcomes to build accountability.
prelimsPointers: GeM is India's national public procurement portal for goods and services.
GFR 2017 governs procurement by central government departments.
QCBS weighs both technical quality and financial cost, unlike pure L1 selection.
static.mainsAngle: The L1 culture in public procurement often trades quality for the lowest quoted price — examine how procurement reform can reconcile cost discipline with execution capability and asset quality.

static.topic: Civil Aviation, Regional Connectivity and Airport Siting
static.syllabusNode: Infrastructure — Civil Aviation
static.whatIsIt: India's civil aviation sector is regulated by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), with Airports Authority of India (AAI) managing most airports. The UDAN regional connectivity scheme, launched in 2016, subsidises regional routes through viability gap funding and airport-charge concessions to make flying affordable on thin routes. New greenfield airports require central clearance and viability assessment.
static.background: UDAN was launched in October 2016 to connect unserved and underserved airports. State support typically includes reduced VAT on aviation turbine fuel, land and security provision. Airport clearances involve the Ministry of Civil Aviation, AAI and DGCA, and competing proposals in the same catchment area can affect each other's viability.
static.geography: Kuppam in Andhra Pradesh lies close to the Tamil Nadu border, while Hosur in Tamil Nadu sits near Bengaluru — overlapping catchments that make the two proposals competing rather than complementary.
static.socioEconomic: Airlines operate on thin margins with aviation turbine fuel a dominant cost, and fuel remains largely outside the GST net; airport proximity in turn shapes regional investment, logistics and real estate.
static.whyInNews: Clearance for an airport at Kuppam in Andhra Pradesh is reported to put Tamil Nadu's proposed Hosur airport in jeopardy, while a parallel commentary argues India must rethink its aviation strategy to make airlines commercially viable.
static.wayForward: Rationalise fuel taxation and airport charges, plan airport capacity on a regional rather than state-by-state basis, and align UDAN route subsidies with demonstrated demand so connectivity does not come at the cost of airline viability.
prelimsPointers: UDAN, the regional connectivity scheme, was launched in 2016.
DGCA is the civil aviation regulator; AAI manages most of India's airports.
Aviation turbine fuel is a major airline cost and largely lies outside the GST framework.
static.mainsAngle: Regional connectivity and airline commercial viability often pull in opposite directions — examine the fiscal, taxation and regulatory levers available to balance the two.

static.topic: India–Nepal Relations and the Neighbourhood First Policy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood (Neighbourhood First)
static.whatIsIt: The bilateral relationship between India and Nepal, structured around the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, an open border, and dense people-to-people, water, energy, trade and security linkages.
static.background: Diplomatic ties are anchored in the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship; water-sharing arrangements include the 1954 Kosi and Gandak agreements and the 1996 Mahakali Treaty. The 2015 constitution and the accompanying Madhesi protests, followed by a prolonged transit disruption, sharply strained ties. The Eminent Persons' Group set up to review the 1950 treaty submitted its report in 2018, but it has not been acted upon. Boundary questions over Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura remain unresolved and are handled through an existing bilateral boundary mechanism.
static.geography: Nepal is landlocked between India and China, sharing borders with Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim; the India-Nepal open border runs roughly 1,750 km and permits visa-free movement of citizens.

stories.headline: Stubble burning counts under scrutiny; new PUC renewal rules take effect
stories.summary: India is grappling with complex environmental challenges, including the persistent issue of stubble burning, where traditional satellite monitoring methods are proving insufficient to accurately gauge the true scale of agricultural fires. Simultaneously, regulatory oversight is tightening with the implementation of new Pollution Under Control (PUC) certificate renewal rules, aiming to enforce stricter compliance regarding vehicle emissions. Beyond local pollution, there is a growing recognition that achieving a comprehensive green transition is not merely an ecological goal but a critical strategic frontier for national development and global competitiveness.
stories.whyItMatters: These developments highlight the intersection of environmental governance, regulatory enforcement, and strategic policy planning, crucial areas for UPSC examination.
